stories.headline: J&K Bank’s Outward Surge: Is J&K Paying the Price?
stories.title: J&K Bank’s Outward Surge: Is J&K Paying the Price?
stories.summary: A striking divergence is emerging in the lending pattern of Jammu and Kashmir Bank as its business outside the Union Territory expands at a much faster pace than its traditional home market. While advances in the Rest of India, including Ladakh, grew 30.9 per cent during 2025-26, lending in J&K increased by 9.3 per cent, raising questions over the changing balance between the bank’s national expansion and growth in its core market. According to the bank’s March 2026 earnings disclosure, gross advances in the Rest of India, including Ladakh, stood at Rs 48,822 crore as on March 31, 2026, accounting for 39.1 per cent of the bank’s total gross advances of Rs 1,24,981 crore. Advances in J&K stood at Rs 76,159 crore, accounting for 60.9 per cent of the total. The growth gap is considerably sharper than the difference in the size of the two portfolios. Advances outside J&K increased from Rs 37,292 crore in March 2025 to Rs 48,822 crore in March 2026, registering growth of 30.9 per cent. In comparison, advances within J&K rose from Rs 69,694 crore to Rs 76,159 crore, representing growth of 9.3 per cent. This means the Rest of India portfolio grew at more than three times the rate of the J&K portfolio during the year. The difference becomes even more pronounced when incremental lending is considered. The bank added Rs 11,530 crore to its Rest of India advances during 2025-26, compared with an increase of Rs 6,465 crore in J&K. Consequently, around 64 per cent of the total increase in gross advances during the year came from the Rest of India portfolio, while only around 36 per cent came from J&K. The bank, however, has attributed part of the slower growth in its home market to the disruption caused by the Pahalgam terror attack and its impact on economic activity. A senior bank official, speaking about the impact of the attack on the local economy, said business activity and credit offtake in key geographies had remained affected following the incident. The bank’s MD and CEO Amitava Chatterjee had also said shortly after the attack that the incident could affect the local economy, although he noted that the bank’s direct exposure to tourism was relatively limited. The composition of lending also highlights the different character of the two markets. Corporate lending accounts for 79 per cent of gross advances in the Rest of India, according to the bank’s disclosure. Personal loans account for 12 per cent, while agriculture, SME and trade constitute 3 per cent, 3 per cent and 2 per cent respectively. In J&K, the portfolio is considerably more diversified. Personal loans account for 49 per cent of gross advances, followed by agriculture at 15 per cent, SME at 14 per cent, trade at 12 per cent and corporate lending at 7 per cent. Thus, the bank’s expansion outside J&K is being driven predominantly by corporate lending, whereas its home-market portfolio has much greater exposure to individual borrowers, agriculture, small businesses and trade. The geographical expansion is also being accompanied by a changing recruitment strategy, according to sources familiar with the bank’s plans. Sources said J&K Bank is moving towards a pan-India recruitment model for positions linked to its operations outside J&K. According to them, vacancies attached to branches in cities such as Delhi would be filled through a wider recruitment pool rather than being restricted to candidates from J&K. “Earlier, regular recruitment was restricted to permanent residents of the erstwhile State of J&K. With the bank’s expansion outside J&K, the recruitment model is also being aligned with the location of its operations,” sources said. The claim, however, needs to be distinguished from the bank’s current apprenticeship programme. The latest apprenticeship notification already provides geographically earmarked positions outside J&K and Ladakh, but apprenticeships are not regular jobs. J&K Bank’s 2026-27 apprenticeship notification provides for 614 positions. Of these, 461 are in J&K, 18 in Ladakh and 135 in locations outside J&K and Ladakh. The bank has separately categorised the latter as “ROI - Vacancy Distribution (outside UT J&K and Ladakh).” The 135 positions outside the two Union Territories include 42 in Delhi, 26 in Mumbai and Greater Mumbai, 20 in Lucknow, 19 in Bengaluru and 28 in Mohali. They account for nearly 22 per cent of the total apprenticeship intake. The present apprenticeship exercise cannot, however, be described as regular employment. The notification provides for a 12-month apprenticeship and states that an apprentice has no right to claim employment with the bank after completion. The recruitment shift being cited by sources would nevertheless represent a significant departure from the bank’s earlier regular recruitment framework. In its 2018 recruitment notification for Banking Associates, J&K Bank had invited applications from “permanent residents of J&K State”. The notification also stated that selected candidates could be posted anywhere in India. Thus, before 2019, eligibility for regular recruitment was linked to permanent residency of the erstwhile State, even though employees recruited through the process could subsequently be posted outside J&K. The present model, if implemented for regular recruitment as described by the sources, would represent a different approach, with recruitment for outside-J&K operations being aligned with the geographical location of the vacancies. The broader transformation in the bank’s geographical footprint is already evident. J&K Bank’s 2024-25 annual report stated that the bank had 1,019 branches, including IARBs, spread across 18 states and four Union Territories as of March 31, 2025. The developments raise a larger question for J&K, where the bank has historically occupied a much more significant position in the financial ecosystem than an ordinary commercial bank.

stories.headline: India's influenza surge seasonal, not new or deadlier strain: Dr Saumya Swaminathan
stories.title: India's influenza surge seasonal, not new or deadlier strain: Dr Saumya Swaminathan
stories.summary: The current rise in influenza cases across parts of India is a routine seasonal uptick rather than the emergence of a novel or more dangerous virus, former Director ICMR Dr. Soumya Swaminathan has said. Speaking to media, Dr Swaminathan said that India is recording a seasonal influenza uptick, and this happens every year. “The doctors feel that this year it has started a little earlier, but normally in India, we do have a monsoon seasonal increase in influenza cases, and then it continues into winter,” she stated while dismissing need for alarm. Dr Swaminathan, who has also served as Chief Scientist at WHO highlighted the improved monitoring as a contributor to a clearer picture of circulating viruses. “Thanks to better surveillance through the government ICMR viral laboratories throughout the year, we actually now know which viruses are circulating, which are predominant. And we can also correlate with clinical presentation, with severity, and with hospital admissions. This is a very good resource,” she said. She said the predominant driver of the present increase is an H1N1 influenza A virus of the Michigan strain. “The current increase in cases is because of H1N1, a Michigan strain. It’s an influenza A virus,” she said. She assed that the same strain that has been circulating since the pandemic in 2009 and this year’s Virus is very similar to what was last year. She reassured people that this is not a new strain. “I think there’s a lot more awareness, more testing, more diagnostics being performed,” she said. She added that more cases are being reported from many hospitals in Delhi, Bengaluru, and other cities due to increased testing. “People might tend to panic, thinking that, you know, there are suddenly thousands of cases. It’s just better testing,” she said. The clarification comes amid a rise in H1N1 cases, particularly in Delhi. Over 1,777 H1N1 cases had been reported by August 20 out of 2,392 Influenza A cases this year. ICMR scientists have said the H1N1 viruses currently circulating in India are similar to the A/Missouri/11/2025 (H1N1)pdm09-like strain. They also said the circulating influenza strains are well matched with the vaccine strains recommended for the Northern Hemisphere. India’s National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) continues to maintain seasonal influenza surveillance. It provides technical guidance on H1N1, including patient categorisation, home care, mask use, clinical management and laboratory testing.

stories.headline: India Inc’s equity fundraising surges past Rs 1.11 lakh crore on strong inflows in July-August
stories.title: India Inc’s equity fundraising surges past Rs 1.11 lakh crore on strong inflows in July-August
stories.summary: Mumbai: Corporate India raised more than ₹1.11 lakh crore through mainboard initial public offerings (IPOs), qualified institutional placements and offers for sale through July and August, as domestic liquidity and improving investor sentiment kept the capital markets active despite range-bound movements in key equity gauges.The two-month fundraising tally is the highest since October-November 2024, when more than ₹1.14 lakh crore was raised through these routes.Read more: Investors’ equity rush helps SIP assets triple in five yearsIPO activity remained particularly strong, garnering more than 40% of the funds raised. So far this month, 20 companies have collected more than ₹20,850 crore, adding on to the ₹28,650 crore raised by 12 companies in July. Listed companies have also stepped up qualified institutional placements (QIP), with four companies raising ₹3,250 crore so far in August, against ₹25,114 crore by eight companies in July.In the offer for sale (OFS) segment, where existing investors cash out in part, Life Insurance Corp of India raised nearly ₹31,447 crore in August to boost public float in the country's biggest institutional investor.133485416Volatility Hit TransactionsAnother public-sector major, Cochin Shipyard, raised nearly ₹1,705 crore in July. "The primary market does not necessarily require a sharply rising index; it requires liquidity, reasonable volatility and confidence in individual companies," said Munish Aggarwal, co-head, investment banking, Equirus Capital.Companies and shareholders had postponed transactions during extreme volatility in the immediate aftermath of the West Asian war.They are now using the improved market window to raise growth capital, reduce debt, finance acquisitions, meet regulatory requirements, and provide exits to promoters and private-equity investors, experts said.The surge in capital-market activity comes even as benchmark indices have remained range-bound. The Sensex and Nifty gained 2.1% and 2.2%, respectively, in July, but have declined 0.5% and 0.7%, respectively, so far in August, as oil prices have hardened yet again.The Nifty MidCap 150 and Nifty SmallCap 250 gained 1.6% and 1.1%, respectively, in July and have risen 1.2% and 2.8%, respectively, so far in August.Aggarwal said equity markets have remained range-bound amid multiple headwinds, including the prolonged West Asia conflict, higher crude and logistics costs, and concerns over the sustainability of IT earnings in the AI era.Domestic institutional and retail flows have provided a counterbalance to uneven overseas purchases, undergirding benchmarks and providing companies with the necessary confidence to tap the capital markets.Retail contributions through systematic investment plans (SIP) stood at approximately ₹31,961 crore in July, while active equity funds received nearly ₹24,700 crore, providing domestic institutions with significant capital to deploy. The broader 2026 numbers underline the strength of the fundraising cycle.

opening: Mumbai: Corporate India raised more than ₹1.11 lakh crore through mainboard initial public offerings (IPOs), qualified institutional placements and offers for sale through July and August, as domestic liquidity and improving investor sentiment kept the capital markets active despite range-bound movements in key equity gauges.
The two-month fundraising tally is the highest since October-November 2024, when more than ₹1.14 lakh crore was raised through these routes.
body: Investors’ equity rush helps SIP assets triple in five yearsIPO activity remained particularly strong, garnering more than 40% of the funds raised.
So far this month, 20 companies have collected more than ₹20,850 crore, adding on to the ₹28,650 crore raised by 12 companies in July.
Listed companies have also stepped up qualified institutional placements (QIP), with four companies raising ₹3,250 crore so far in August, against ₹25,114 crore by eight companies in July.

In the offer for sale (OFS) segment, where existing investors cash out in part, Life Insurance Corp of India raised nearly ₹31,447 crore in August to boost public float in the country's biggest institutional investor.
Volatility Hit TransactionsAnother public-sector major, Cochin Shipyard, raised nearly ₹1,705 crore in July.

"The primary market does not necessarily require a sharply rising index; it requires liquidity, reasonable volatility and confidence in individual companies," said Munish Aggarwal, co-head, investment banking, Equirus Capital.
Companies and shareholders had postponed transactions during extreme volatility in the immediate aftermath of the West Asian war.

They are now using the improved market window to raise growth capital, reduce debt, finance acquisitions, meet regulatory requirements, and provide exits to promoters and private-equity investors, experts said.
The surge in capital-market activity comes even as benchmark indices have remained range-bound.
The Sensex and Nifty gained 2.1% and 2.2%, respectively, in July, but have declined 0.5% and 0.7%, respectively, so far in August, as oil prices have hardened yet again.

Aggarwal said equity markets have remained range-bound amid multiple headwinds, including the prolonged West Asia conflict, higher crude and logistics costs, and concerns over the sustainability of IT earnings in the AI era.

Domestic institutional and retail flows have provided a counterbalance to uneven overseas purchases, undergirding benchmarks and providing companies with the necessary confidence to tap the capital markets.

Retail contributions through systematic investment plans (SIP) stood at approximately ₹31,961 crore in July, while active equity funds received nearly ₹24,700 crore, providing domestic institutions with significant capital to deploy.
The broader 2026 numbers underline the strength of the fundraising cycle.

Retail contributions through systematic investment plans (SIP) stood at approximately ₹31,961 crore in July, while active equity funds received nearly ₹24,700 crore, providing domestic institutions with significant capital to deploy.

stories.headline: Sebi drops Rs 3,912-cr probe against Max Fin, Axis Bank
stories.title: Sebi drops Rs 3,912-cr probe against Max Fin, Axis Bank
stories.summary: Mumbai: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has dropped proceedings against Max Financial Services, Max Life Insurance Company, Axis Bank and other Axis group entities, concluding that allegations of disclosure lapses and a fraudulent scheme that allegedly caused a ₹3,912-crore loss to Max Financial and its shareholders couldn't be proved. The market regulator has also cleared Max Financial founder Analjit Singh, besides former and current senior executives named in the proceedings.The case stems from Sebi's probe into a series of transactions between Max Financial, Max Life, and Axis entities between FY10 and FY22. The regulator had examined three sets of arrangements-in 2010, 2015 and 2020-relating to the issue, sale and subsequent acquisition of shares in Max Life.Read more: SoftBank pares nearly 2.6% stake in Lenskart for Rs 2,888 croreFollowing the investigation, Sebi issued a show cause notice on October 24, 2024 alleging that the transactions were structured to provide Axis Bank benefits beyond permissible commission limits for its role as a corporate agent. It had also alleged that Max Financial made inadequate and delayed disclosures and that the arrangements formed part of a fraudulent scheme that benefited Axis entities at the expense of Max Financial and its shareholders."... the disclosures made by MFSL (Max Financial Services) could undoubtedly have been more comprehensive and, in certain instances, a more cautious and consistent approach to disclosure may have been desirable," said Sebi whole time member Amarjeet Singh.
